s491: Foreign holders generally owe no U.S. tax on gains from selling Class A shares. Exceptions apply when the gain is tied to a U.S. business, when the seller is in the U.S. 183 days or more that year, or in a real property rule that Anthropic says should not apply to it.
s492: Anthropic reports dividends and any tax withheld to the IRS, which may share the information with a holder's home country. Payments can face 24% backup withholding unless the holder certifies foreign status on a W-8 form. This withholding is a credit against tax owed, not an extra tax.
s493: Under FATCA, a U.S. law aimed at hidden foreign accounts, dividends paid to foreign financial institutions or other foreign entities that do not meet U.S. reporting rules face 30% withholding. Proposed rules exempt sale proceeds for now.

s341: Public shareholders will have little control over Anthropic: an independent Long-Term Benefit Trust elects a board majority, and a single founder-held Class F share carries 50.1% of all votes, so the two together pick the whole board and approve any sale. s84: Anthropic's biggest exposure here is copyright: it agreed in September 2025 to pay $1.5B to settle the Bartz class action, still faces suits from music publishers and Reddit, and courts have not settled whether AI training is fair use. It has also suffered security breaches, and theft of its model weights could erase its competitive edge.
s258: Anthropic, maker of Claude, grew quarterly revenue to $11.6B in the three months ended June 30, 2026, from $787 million a year earlier, and turned an operating profit, but has huge compute commitments stretching to 2045. It faces OpenAI and Google, a $1.5B authors' copyright settlement, and U.S. government restrictions on some models.
s376: Anthropic's top executives were paid modestly in cash in 2025 but heavily in stock, with totals of $17,958,298 for Dario Amodei and $16,408,998 for Daniela Amodei, including millions for security. root: Anthropic, maker of Claude, is going public on Nasdaq as "ANT" with revenue of $16.286B in the six months ended June 30, 2026, but a $80.748B net loss, mostly a paper charge, and compute commitments of about $265.6B. Class A buyers get little control: the co-founders hold 50.1% of votes and a trust elects a board majority.
